name: Hammam

card.summary: A humid steam-bath ritual of heat, scrubbing and washing that leaves skin visibly cleaner and smoother, used as a regular skin and grooming routine.
card.note: Heat exposure and vigorous scrubbing; people with heart conditions, low blood pressure or sensitive skin are usually advised to take care.

quick.overview:
The hammam is a traditional bathing ritual of Middle Eastern, North African and Ottoman origin in which a person moves through progressively hotter, steam-filled rooms to sweat, then is scrubbed and washed, often with a rough mitt called a kese, and finishes with a rinse and sometimes a massage.

For appearance, the draw is the scrub: exfoliating the surface of the skin leaves it smoother and brighter, and the steam softens skin beforehand. Research on hammam is limited and covers other outcomes, such as a trial in women with endometriosis-related pain and a small study in dialysis patients, and one randomised trial that tested whether the scrub changes sunburn susceptibility.
quick.how: A visit typically starts in a warm room, moves to a hot, steamy room and often a heated marble platform, and then an attendant, or the bather, scrubs the skin with a kese mitt and soap before a warm rinse. Modern spas offer the same sequence as a treatment, sometimes with a clay mask, oils or a massage added. Many people schedule it every week or two as part of a grooming routine.
quick.risks: Prolonged heat can cause dizziness and dehydration, and clinical advice usually cautions people with heart disease, low blood pressure or pregnancy to ask a doctor first. Vigorous scrubbing can irritate sensitive skin or skin with eczema or rosacea. A randomised trial found that a hammam scrub did not make healthy volunteers more prone to sunburn.

lead: The hammam is a bathing institution that descends from Roman and Greek public baths and developed in the early Islamic world, with Umayyad-era examples in Syria and Jordan among the earliest known.[1] It spread across the Middle East, North Africa, al-Andalus, Central Asia, South Asia and the Balkans, and Ottoman builders such as Mimar Sinan produced many of Istanbul's best-known examples.[1]

Bathers undress to a wrap or loincloth, pass from a cooler room into warmer and hotter rooms to sweat, and are washed by an attendant of the same sex using soap and vigorous rubbing with a scrubbing mitt, then rinsed with warm water and sometimes massaged.[1][2] The cleansing and exfoliation are what people cite as the skin benefit: a review of the Unani tradition describes hammam as aiming at physical, psychological and cosmetic health through integral cleansing.[3]

Modern studies examine hammam in narrow contexts, including a randomised trial of a hammam and Swedish massage program in women with endometriosis-related pelvic pain,[4] a pilot of sweating therapies in haemodialysis patients,[5] and a randomised trial of whether hammam scrubbing changes sunburn.[6]

angle.text: The scrub physically removes dead surface cells, so skin looks and feels smoother right after a visit. People also treat the session as a periodic body-grooming routine, often adding clay masks and oils.

paras: The classical layout follows the Roman model of an undressing room, a cold room, a warm room and a hot room, heated by furnaces and underfloor hypocaust systems; Ottoman baths often merged or dropped the cold room and centred the hot room on a heated marble table called a gobektasi.[1] Domes with small skylights let in light and released steam.[1]

The washing sequence uses a kese mitt and a peshtemal wrap as traditional accessories, and may end with a vigorous massage that can include joint cracking.[1] The term Turkish bath is described as a label popularised by foreign travel writers, first recorded in English in 1644.[2]

Early Islamic scholars debated hammams, with some Maliki scholars opposing them, though objections faded by the ninth century, and some medieval Muslim physicians endorsed them as therapy.[1] Women's hours became common around the tenth century, and women's hammams served as places for socialising, celebrations and matchmaking.[1][2]

Use declined in the early twentieth century as indoor plumbing spread. Cairo is estimated to have had about 77 operating hammams in the early nineteenth century and eight by the early twenty-first, while some in Turkey and Morocco still serve locals and tourists.[1] A Victorian-era publication presented the Turkish bath as a mode of cure and source of strength, drawing on the writings of David Urquhart.[7]

Unani medicine describes hammam-i-Bukhari as a regimen that reduces the viscosity of humours and draws morbid matter to the skin surface, and its modern reviewers say it promotes physical, psychological and cosmetic health.[3] Spa operators market the experience for glowing, exfoliated skin.

A randomised trial of 44 women with endometriosis-related chronic pelvic pain tested a four-week programme combining hammam hydrotherapy and Swedish massage against a control group, measuring pain, well-being and quality of life.[4] A two-centre crossover pilot in haemodialysis patients found that stimulated sweating, in hot baths or a hammam centre, was associated with lower interdialytic weight gain.[5]

A randomised paired-design trial in healthy adults with skin types 1 to 3 tested whether a hammam treatment on one side of the back made skin more susceptible to sunburn from natural ultraviolet radiation, and reported no effect.[6] A study compared irisin levels after 45 minutes in a Turkish bath at about 47 degrees Celsius with moderate running in obese and normal-weight men.[8]

timeline.event: Early Islamic hammams appear in the Umayyad period, with Qusayr 'Amra in Jordan among the earliest known.[1]
The term Turkish bath is first recorded in English.[2]
A British medical review publishes a manual of the Turkish bath drawing on Urquhart's writings.[7]
